decisions.reason: “Alarm bells” keeps the warning image; “twisted away” is natural and preserves the evasive action.
Dropping “that” preserves the reference to the strike without changing its meaning.
The clipped phrasing keeps the contrast and suits the abrupt sensation.
It preserves the opposing pains and the accompanying unanswerable question in natural English.
The question is incorporated into the preceding sentence, so its meaning is retained without repetition.
The following sentence supplies the corpse-pale comparison; “white hand” accurately renders the explicit image.
It preserves the corpse-pale hand and the revelation that its owner should have been dead.
“Forcing the words out” and “should never have seen again” keep the strained delivery and forbidden sight.
“Clearly dead” preserves the source’s assertion that his breathing had stopped.
“Yes, I was” answers the question about being dead naturally and faithfully.
It preserves the calm voice and absence of pain without the awkward “free of” construction.
The pronoun clearly refers to the Demon Lord in context; omitting the repeated title loses no information.
“Palm Force” identifies the palm attack, and the sentence retains the near-simultaneous movement.
“The first blow” and “this one” preserve the sequence and explain why he cannot fully evade the follow-up.
“Dimmed” naturally conveys the brief loss of clarity in his vision.
“Kh” renders the brief exertion sound without adding the baseline’s unspoken “Damn.”
The pronoun keeps Jeok Cheongang as the subject from the surrounding passage; the defensive qi and recoil remain intact.
It keeps the scream and the fragments from what his hurtling body struck, in tighter prose.
The hypothetical phrasing preserves that the attack could incapacitate even a Supreme Peak master.
The following line’s “But” retains the contrast without the redundant setup.
It retains the contrast and identifies him as the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang.
The source says his foot touches down and Jeok Cheongang’s form makes the furrow; SOL incorrectly makes his plural feet carve it.
The source specifies congested blood rising with his internal injuries; SOL omits that detail.
“Couldn’t see it” preserves the inability to see the attack and contrasts naturally with sensing it.
Removing “down” does not change the strike’s direction or target.
It preserves that he anticipates the scene half a beat ahead and reacts by pushing off.
“A sliver of an instant” and “huge crater” retain the near miss and scale of the impact.
It preserves the predator-and-prey image and the continuation of the pursuit.
“Closed the distance” is a natural rendering of rapidly erasing the gap.
It retains the light’s dreadful brilliance, its swelling, and Jeok Cheongang’s reaction.
“Then” preserves the sequence from faint pain to the taste of blood.
The subject remains clear from context, and the line preserves his returning vision, sharper pain, and gathering of internal energy.
“Barely under his control” naturally conveys the source’s unstable control.
SOL adds “along with everything else”; the source says the fire dragon might burn its master’s body.
The source leaves the object of devouring implicit; SOL specifies “him,” while BASE preserves the broader image.
“Strange power” preserves the meaning without the stiffer “bizarre power.”
It keeps the unwavering gaze and lava-like voice in fluent prose.
It preserves the unspoken words and the Scorching Yang Qi surging through his body.
“A roar like a dragon’s” preserves the comparison while avoiding the redundant “bellow.”
It joins the interrupted description to the next clause while retaining the unprecedented energy and swallowed retreat order.
The retreat order is retained in the preceding combined sentence, including Jeong Hogun’s name.
“Heard a voice” keeps the sound reaching Jeok Cheongang in the blinding flash.
The introductory sentence is redundant with the following moments and its omission loses no source detail.
It preserves the sensation that the world has stopped.
It retains the shock and roar numbing every sense without the repeated “Moments when.”
It preserves the narrator’s immediate experience; “exactly” adds no necessary meaning.
The hypothetical sun falling in front of the narrator remains intact.
“Force” preserves the impending impact’s meaning while the sentence retains the narrator’s protective action.
It preserves uncertainty about whether the shout reached them and whether they dropped in response.
“On their feet” naturally preserves the consequence of even a moment’s hesitation.
“Heaved” and “flew” retain the upheaval and scattered bluestone fragments in clear action prose.
It preserves the dead bodies and scattered weapons swept up alongside the fragments.
“Took the shock wave with my whole body” preserves the narrator’s braced endurance.
It keeps the depleted energy and the two actions of knocking aside or cutting through incoming objects.
The source says the fragments grazed and scraped him; “slashed across me” intensifies and changes the injury.
“Had to be hurt” preserves the narrator’s willingness to take the unavoidable injury.
The next line establishes that what he saw was Jeok Cheongang shifting position.
“Block the direction we were heading” preserves his move to shield their path.
The present-tense question keeps the narrator’s immediate uncertainty.
“After what felt like an eternity” preserves the duration and the fading roar and impact.
It retains objects falling from the air and the return of sounds after they had gone muffled.
“Save me” naturally completes the plea to be spared.
It retains the fallen from both sides and the desperate plea for life.
“Familiar voices” preserves the recognition without the unnecessary article.
“By thinking about” preserves Taishan’s resolve and the five-spice pork joke.
It keeps the request to break the man’s teeth while making the question more direct.
The split preserves his exhaustion and difficulty answering Namho.
It preserves his staggering and the two people reaching to steady him by the arms.
The undead army is carried into the next paragraph, and “long look” preserves the pointed, questioning glare.
It retains the undead army, the stone wall, and the distance in jang.
It preserves the guards’ losses and the monsters’ sudden attack in direct, natural prose.
It preserves the narrator’s uncertainty about whether luring them would have caused damage.
It retains both examples of the undead rising despite severe injuries.
It preserves that “monster” applies beyond grotesque appearances or strange powers.
“Anything that defied common sense” preserves the source’s definition of a monster.
It retains the Fire King’s inclusion among the monsters in a natural recast.
It preserves Hyuk Mujin’s attempt to stop him and his quick move toward Jeok Cheongang.
The source makes Jeok Cheongang’s words the interruption that prevents the approach; SOL drops that causal, suspenseful setup.
“Deeper than usual” preserves the changed quality of his voice.
SOL places Jeok Cheongang ahead of the narrator; the source places the narrator a few steps behind him.
“Lone figure” and the settling dust preserve the image; “upright” is not needed to convey it.
SOL adds that the figure is walking toward them, a direction the source does not specify.
“Without meaning to” preserves the involuntary intake of breath.
It retains the brief proximity and the absence of any sensed sign of life.
The source says blood already pooled to his ankles splashes with each step; SOL makes it sound as if the step pools the blood.
The source identifies the limbs as belonging to an unknown person; SOL drops that uncertainty.
“Chilling” naturally preserves the figure’s more dreadful atmosphere than the surrounding gore.
It preserves the still-burning face and the lips’ gentle smile in clear sentences.
The source still calls him “he,” though no longer human; SOL replaces him with “the thing.”
It preserves the melted skin and exposed bones without unnecessary wording.
It retains the horrific state, the implied fatal appearance, and his gaze at Jeok Cheongang and the narrator.
“And then he spoke” preserves the transition without overstating the surprise.
It preserves the long-unheard voice reaching the narrator in the moment.
It retains the figure’s staggered rise as the answer is given.
It preserves Ma Sanbao removing the spear and approaching, with “muttered” fitting Jeok Cheongang’s quiet words.
The source says the Demon Lord stepped forward while continuing to speak; SOL drops the continued-speaking cue.
The source says the Master became a parent to him; SOL changes this to simply being a parent.
“Defending their sect’s home” preserves the protective action and the senseless oppression.
“A past long gone” preserves the contrast between the Emperor before him and the vanished past.
The source says he had no choice but to lose them; SOL removes that compulsion.
The source frames where he belonged as a question in the narrator’s realization; SOL turns it into asserted knowledge.
It retains the groan-like delivery and the words slipping from his lips.
